levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
Your organization has detected suspicious activity on one of its Linux servers. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor named UPSTYLE. Your task is to investigate, analyze, and respond to this cybersecurity incident.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Identify and investigate unauthorized or suspicious services running on a host.
- Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.
- Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content:
While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate the running services on the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services.

**Hint:**
Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

**Question:**
What is the name of the suspicious service running on the target host?
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any services that seem out of place or unfamiliar. The suspicious service in this case is `bkd.service`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content:
Now that you have identified the suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after a system reboot. This will help you understand the persistence mechanism used by the attacker.

**Hint:**
Investigate the systemd service files and timers to find how the service is scheduled to run.

**Question:**
What is the name of the systemd timer responsible for starting the suspicious service?
levels.solution: To determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after a system reboot, you can use the `systemctl list-timers` command to list all systemd timers. Look for any timers that seem out of place or unfamiliar. The systemd timer responsible for starting the suspicious service in this case is `lab-checkin.timer`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate the systemd service files and timers to find how the service is scheduled to run.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `systemctl list-timers` command to list all systemd timers.

levels.title: Suspicious File Discovery
levels.content:
Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service. This will help you gather more information about the backdoor and its behavior.

**Hint:**
Check the service unit file to find the path of the executable or script being run.

**Question:**
What is the path of the executable or script associated with the suspicious service?
levels.solution: To locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl cat bkd.service` command to view the service unit file. Look for the `ExecStart` line to find the path of the executable or script being run. The path of the executable or script associated with the suspicious service in this case is `/usr/local/bin/lab-checkin.sh`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the service unit file to find the path of the executable or script being run.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `systemctl cat bkd.service` command to view the service unit file.
